# How to Retrieve Files from Microsoft Forms and Send Them by Email with Power Automate

## Step-by-Step Flow Explanation

In this tutorial, you'll build a Power Automate flow that automatically retrieves every file uploaded through **Microsoft Forms** and sends them as email attachments.

The goal is simple: whenever a new response is submitted, all form data and uploaded documents are collected and delivered in a single, organized email.

---

## Flow Overview

```text
Microsoft Forms
        │
        ▼
When a new response is submitted
        │
        ▼
Get response details
        │
        ▼
Organize uploaded documents
        │
        ▼
Parse JSON
        │
        ▼
Apply to each
        │
        ▼
Get file content
        │
        ▼
Add files to attachment collection
        │
        ▼
Prepare attachments
        │
        ▼
Send email
```

---

## Step 1 — Receive a New Response

The flow starts whenever a new Microsoft Forms response is submitted.

Add the following actions:

* **When a new response is submitted**
* **Get response details**

The first action triggers the flow automatically.

The second retrieves every answer submitted in the form, including file upload fields.

---

## Step 2 — Create an Attachment Collection

Before retrieving any files, create a place to store them.

Add the **Initialize variable** action.

Configure it as follows:

| Setting  | Value         |
| -------- | ------------- |
| **Name** | `Attachments` |
| **Type** | `Array`       |

During the flow execution, every uploaded file will be added to this collection.

---

## Step 3 — Organize the Uploaded Documents

Each file upload field is returned separately by Microsoft Forms.

To simplify processing, group every upload field into a single JSON collection.

Add a **Compose** action containing a structure similar to the example below.

```json
[
  {
    "Type": "Document 1",
    "Response": "Upload Field 1"
  },
  {
    "Type": "Document 2",
    "Response": "Upload Field 2"
  }
]
```

Each object represents one upload field from your Microsoft Form.

> **Important**
>
> The field identifiers shown in this example are unique to each Microsoft Form.
> Always use the dynamic content generated by your own form.

<p align="center">
<img src="../../images/github/json.png" alt="JSON structure" width="900">
</p>

---

## Step 4 — Parse the JSON

At this point, Power Automate still treats the uploaded file information as plain text.

To access each property individually, add a **Parse JSON** action.

**Content**

Use the output from the **Compose** action.

**Schema**

Paste the schema that matches the JSON created in the previous step.

After parsing, Power Automate can access properties such as:

* File name
* File ID
* File path
* Other metadata returned by Microsoft Forms

---

## Step 5 — Process Each Uploaded File

Since a form can contain multiple uploaded files, each document must be processed individually.

Add an **Apply to each** action.

As its input, use the output from **Parse JSON**.

All remaining actions will be created inside this loop.

<p align="center">
<img src="../../images/github/compor.png" alt="Apply to each" width="900">
</p>

---

## Step 6 — Retrieve the File Identifier

Inside the **Apply to each** loop, add a **Compose** action.

This expression checks whether a file exists.

If a file is available, it returns its identifier.

Otherwise, it returns the text **FILE**, preventing the flow from failing when an upload field is empty.

```text
@if(...)
```

This identifier will be used in the next step to retrieve the actual file.

---

## Step 7 — Generate the Attachment Name

Add another **Compose** action.

This expression automatically generates the attachment name.

Example:

```text
Document1.pdf
Document2.jpg
Document3.png
```

Using standardized names makes the email attachments easier to identify.

---

## Step 8 — Check Whether a File Exists

Add a **Condition** action.

Configure it to verify whether the output from the first **Compose** action is different from **FILE**.

* **True** → A file exists and should be processed.
* **False** → No file was uploaded. The flow skips this item and continues.

This validation prevents unnecessary errors.

---

## Step 9 — Retrieve the File Content

Inside the **True** branch, add the **Get file content** action.

Use the identifier returned by the first **Compose** action as the **File Identifier**.

At this point, Power Automate retrieves the complete file from Microsoft 365.

---

## Step 10 — Add the File to the Attachment Collection

Still inside the **True** branch, add the **Append to array variable** action.

Select the **Attachments** variable created earlier.

In the **Value** field, use a structure similar to the following:

```json
{
  "Name": "...",
  "ContentBytes": "..."
}
```

Repeat this process for every uploaded file.

Once the **Apply to each** loop finishes, the **Attachments** array will contain every file submitted through the form.

---

## Step 11 — Prepare the Attachments

After all files have been added to the collection, create two more actions:

* **Compose**
* **Parse JSON**

These actions convert the attachment collection into the format expected by Outlook.

<p align="center">
<img src="../../images/github/fim.png" alt="Preparing attachments" width="900">
</p>

---

## Step 12 — Send the Email

Finally, add the **Send an email (V2)** action.

Configure it as usual:

* Recipient
* Subject
* Email Body

In the **Attachments** field, use the output from the final **Parse JSON** action.

Outlook will automatically attach every file collected during the flow.

<p align="center">
<img src="../../images/github/e-mail.png" alt="Email result" width="900">
</p>

---

## Result

After the flow finishes, the recipient receives a single email containing:

* All Microsoft Forms responses;
* Every uploaded document;
* Automatically organized attachments;
* Files ready for review.

---
